doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

chapter: Sarah Vaughan's band on the road
title: Stranded in Las Vegas and the union's power
summary: Sarah's husband left the band unpaid; Hy Jaffe of the union forced tickets; union power versus today; then Carmen McRae.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Did you ever have any hassles in different parts of the country traveling with that particular group?

No. Not with Sarah. With Al Hibbler. But right after Sarah, right after I left Sarah, and that was not a very good way to leave anybody— Sarah had a husband at that time, his name was C.B. Atkins. And he left us stranded. Didn’t pay us the last week in the hotel in Las Vegas, and didn’t get an airplane ticket for us to get out of there. So they just left. Well of course we stayed and we called the union back in New York and Hy Jaffe was the treasurer at that time. And he called Sarah’s house and he told C.B. if he didn’t get a ticket out to Las Vegas immediately, this was like just the same weekend, if he didn’t get a ticket out to Las Vegas, Sarah would never work in the United States again. We got a call from Western Union that same night, said our plane tickets, the money and everything is here at the Western Union, your tickets are here. So Hy Jaffe was serious. He was power. And he probably could have stopped her from working just like that, because they didn’t take any stuff from anybody. That’s why the union was powerful at that time. This was like 1963. Now, people do anything they want to do. Anything. There is no power. But see times have changed so much and nobody’s even noticed it. It wasn’t that they were overlords or anything like that, it was that they looked out for the musicians. By the same token, the musicians had to take care of themselves. Sarah was part of the union. She was a pianist you know. You probably know that she got her start working with Earl Hines and Billy Eckstine playing piano in a Earl Hines’ band. So they wouldn’t stand for her husband or manager mistreating the musicians. So we had tickets that night.
